tagline.text: A palm-sized primate blinking huge eyes in the forest

children.text: A sanctuary in the forests of Corella, Bohol, where you can observe the Philippine tarsier — one of the world's smallest primates — in its natural habitat. Following a guide along a short forest trail, you can quietly meet tarsiers napping while clinging to tree branches.

The Philippine tarsier, commonly known simply as the "tarsier," is a tiny primate about 10–15cm long and weighing around 100–150g. It's distinguished by a tail longer than its body, slender fingers, and two enormous eyes that take up half its face — each eyeball is roughly the size of its brain. Unable to roll its eyes, it instead turns its head nearly 180 degrees to look behind it, and at night it leaps among branches hunting insects. It's endemic to the southern Philippine islands of Bohol, Samar, Leyte, and Mindanao.
Bohol's foremost place to see tarsiers is the Philippine Tarsier Sanctuary in Corella. Established in the late

by the Philippine Tarsier Foundation, it grew out of the lifelong research and conservation work of a local known as the "Tarsier Man," Carlito Pizarras. The scientific genus name of the Philippine tarsier, "Carlito," is in fact taken from his name.

The sanctuary isn't a cage or a display facility — it's the forest itself. During the day, tarsiers sleep among branches or vines; staff check their locations each morning and then guide visitors along a short forest trail. Only a handful of individuals can typically be seen at a time, but the experience of watching one open and blink its huge eyes, or turn its head, at close range is far more striking than you might expect.
The visit is short, around
30 minutes

, and the trail is flat, so it's manageable for children and elderly visitors alike. It's a must-see along with the Chocolate Hills and the Loboc River on a Bohol countryside tour, and travelers who care about animal welfare should choose a foundation-run sanctuary like this one over roadside facilities that crowd animals into cramped spaces.
An entrance ticket comes with a staff member guiding you along the forest trail and pointing out the branches where tarsiers are sleeping. You'll typically see around four to eight in sequence.

The visitor center at the entrance has panels and photos introducing tarsier ecology, diet, breeding, and conservation efforts. Browsing them before your walk makes what you see in the forest more interesting.
The rule is to shoot with flash off and in silent mode. Using a camera's telephoto function or a smartphone's 2–3x zoom lets you get clear photos without getting too close.
Proceeds from entrance fees and souvenir sales go toward habitat protection and research. Buying a tarsier plush toy or T-shirt at the foundation's gift shop also supports the conservation work.

Ask your guide why tarsiers sleep during the day, how far they can jump, and what they eat, and you'll hear some vivid stories. Their ability to jump several dozen times their own body length in a single leap is especially astonishing.

blocks.title: Pairing it with a countryside tour

children.text: Corella is close to Tagbilaran and sits on the route to Loboc and the Chocolate Hills, making it a good first stop on a day tour.

blocks.title: Seeing Baclayon Church and the Blood Compact Shrine together

children.text: Near the road from Tagbilaran to Corella are the Blood Compact Shrine, commemorating the
blood pact between the Spanish explorer Legazpi and Bohol chieftain Sikatuna, and Baclayon Church, one of the oldest stone churches in the Philippines, built of coral stone. Both can be seen in about
30 minutes
each, making them good stops before or after the tarsier visit.

Most travelers visit by countryside tour vehicle (about
per car starting from Panglao). Some tour packages take visitors to a different tarsier facility near Loboc instead of Corella, so tell your driver beforehand which one you want.
Tarsiers can be observed year-round, but the dry season,
December–May
, is most pleasant, with dry trails and clear skies. During the rainy season,
June–November
, trails get slippery and mosquitoes increase, and viewing is sometimes suspended on days of heavy rain.

There is almost no accommodation near the sanctuary, so it's standard to base yourself in Alona Beach on Panglao Island or in Tagbilaran city and visit for the day. Alona Beach resorts run about
or more a night, and Tagbilaran city hotels run about
. For a quiet stay in nature, you could also stay at a bungalow along the Loboc River and visit the sanctuary early the next morning.

The sanctuary entrance only has a kiosk selling drinks and simple snacks. For meals, use the Loboc River lunch cruise buffet or restaurants in Tagbilaran city. Tagbilaran has an old shopping mall (such as Island City Mall) with a food court and local seafood restaurants, good for a meal before or after the tour. Bohol specialty snacks calamay and piaya are popular souvenirs.
There's no ATM near the sanctuary. Prepare cash for the entrance fee and souvenirs.
On the forest trail, moving in a single file and keeping your voice down is the rule. It helps to explain to children beforehand why they need to be quiet.
Tarsiers sit in shady spots between branches, so photos can come out dark. Turn off your smartphone's night mode and raise the exposure slightly instead.
There are mosquitoes, so long pants and repellent help.
Forest-trail soil is slippery after rain, so wear shoes with soles rather than sandals.
A countryside tour driver might steer you to a different roadside facility, claiming it's cheaper. If animal welfare matters to you, ask for the foundation-run sanctuary.
Operating hours are generally
9:00 AM to 4:00 PM
, with last entry around
. If you put it as the last stop of a countryside tour, it's easy to miss entry time, so drop by in the morning.
Tarsiers are extremely sensitive to noise, light, and touch, and stress can harm their health. Never touch them or use flash, and don't make loud noises.
Feeding tarsiers or shaking their branches is prohibited.
Pushing a selfie stick in close for a shot is also prohibited. Observe only from the distance set by your guide.
The Philippine tarsier is a species needing protection due to habitat loss. Avoid any place where individuals are privately bought, sold, or kept as pets.
Operating hours and entry rules can change depending on the foundation, so check the latest notices before visiting.
